meanings.note: Common Russian noun meaning 'kids; guys' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Тогда ребята с тобой поработают. До свидания, Аркадий Борисович.
examples.trans: Then the boys will have a little word with you. Goodbye, Arkady Borisovich.
Then the boys will have a little word with you.
Right, kids, go out of the room.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'well; come on', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Oh, come on, Dad!
Well?

examples.text: Ну что, очкарик? Видишь, ничего не осталось.
examples.trans: Well, four-eyes? See, there's nothing left.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to give; (imperative) let's', paired with 'дать'.

examples.trans: Let's talk.
He gives me a book.

examples.text: Давай мы его уволим, а тебя на его место назначим.
examples.trans: Let's fire him and put you in his place.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'what', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: What's this?
Look what I've got.

examples.text: Привет! Смотри, что у меня есть.
examples.trans: Hi! Look what I've got.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'not', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Chef, I didn't take it.
I don't know.
There wasn't enough money.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'дать'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'gave up, ratted out'.

examples.text: Нам надо сдать машину до десяти часов.
examples.trans: We have to return the car before ten o'clock.

examples.text: Я за комнаткой пригляжу. Может, сдам кому, а денежки пополам!
examples.trans: I'll look after the little room. Maybe I'll rent it to someone, and we'll split the money!

examples.text: Может, сдам кому, а денежки пополам!
examples.trans: Maybe I'll rent it to someone, and we'll split the money!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'something; somehow', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Has something happened?
Somehow I'm tired.
I can't see it somehow.

meanings.note: Prefix 'на-' marks surface contact, accumulation, or completing a quantity (stem 'бираться'). Reflexive/intransitive verb with the postfix '-ся'/'-сь' (historically from the reflexive pronoun 'себя', oneself). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to gather, accumulate'.

examples.trans: We are still coming up short.

examples.text: На кухне никто не хочет набираться без причины.
examples.trans: In the kitchen nobody wants to gather without a reason.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'to you', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Dad, did you bring any gum?
And this is for you. A toy car!

examples.text: У тебя же есть ещё. Дай хоть одну.
examples.trans: But you've still got some. Give me just one.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian clause-linking conjunction meaning 'and, but; so', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: And this is for you.
And where's the toy car?
Dad, did you bring any gum?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'yes, indeed', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Oh yeah?
Yes, it's me.
Oh yeah? When?

meanings.note: Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.trans: Lyolya will definitely come!

examples.text: Я точно не помню его адрес.
examples.trans: I don't remember his exact address.

examples.text: Точно, полиция была! А что с машиной?
examples.trans: That's right, the police were there! And what about the car?

meanings.note: Prefix 'от-' ('away from, off') marks separation, completion, or response (stem 'бороздить'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to sail across, plow through'.

related.gloss: not to to sail across (negated infinitive)

examples.trans: Senka has sailed his last boat.

examples.text: На кухне никто не хочет отбороздить без причины.
examples.trans: In the kitchen nobody wants to sail across without a reason.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'my own', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: А что я за мэр такой, который держит своё слово?
examples.trans: And what kind of mayor would I be if I kept my word?

examples.text: Ты преподавай. А они пусть строят свои торговые центры.
examples.trans: You teach. And let them build their shopping centres.

examples.text: А они пусть строят свои торговые центры.
examples.trans: And let them build their shopping centres.

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'launch, boat' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Senka has sailed his last boat.

examples.text: На нашей кухне уже есть новый баркас.
examples.trans: In our kitchen there is already a new launch.

meanings.note: Prefix 'про-' indicates movement through, completion, or missing the mark (stem 'щать'). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to forgive; bid farewell'.

examples.trans: All the best. Farewell!

examples.text: Тогда прощай, я должен срочно уйти.
examples.trans: Then farewell, I must urgently leave.
Farewell, our old communal apartment!

meanings.note: Abstract feminine noun formed with the Slavic suffix '-ость' ('-ness, -ity') from the corresponding adjective. Common feminine noun meaning 'bone' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: To break his bones.

examples.text: Я пойду и переломаю ему кости!
examples.trans: I will go and break his bones!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'this, that; it is', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: That's mine.
And this is for you.
And this is for you. A toy car!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronominal determiner meaning 'my, mine', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Where's my toy car?
That's mine.
No. That's mine.

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'briefs, underwear' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Kostya, those are not my panties.

examples.text: На нашей кухне уже есть новый трусики.
examples.trans: In our kitchen there is already a new briefs.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to see', paired with 'увидеть'.

examples.trans: I can see the toy car.

examples.text: Ну что, очкарик? Видишь, ничего не осталось.
examples.trans: Well, four-eyes? See, there's nothing left.
See the markers? They're from Japan!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'there', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Everything's fine there.
Who's there?
Hello! How was it in Hungary?

meanings.note: Prefix 'раз-' ('apart, un-, thoroughly') indicates distribution or intensive action (stem 'вешивать'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to hang up'.

related.gloss: not to to hang up (negated infinitive)

examples.text: Тебе там развешивала белье в ванной?
examples.trans: Were you the one hanging laundry in the bathroom?

examples.text: На кухне никто не хочет развешивать без причины.
examples.trans: In the kitchen nobody wants to hang up without a reason.

meanings.note: Common neuter noun meaning 'linen, laundry; underwear' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: У него даже постельного белья нет.
examples.trans: He doesn't even have bed linen.
Clean linen is in the wardrobe.

examples.text: Клавдия Викторовна, вы со всей квартиры бельё принесли! У меня уже спина болит.
examples.trans: Klavdia Viktorovna, you brought laundry from the whole flat! My back is hurting already.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'in, into', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: How is it in Hungary?
I grew up in a communal flat.
Hello! How was it in Hungary?

meanings.note: Common feminine noun meaning 'bathtub, bath' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: The carp live in the bathtub.
They live wonderfully in the bathtub.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'лушать'). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to listen', paired with 'послушать'.

examples.trans: Listen, Samson.
Yes, I'm listening.

examples.text: Слушай, Самсон, я тут подумал. Твой начальник — такой опытный специалист.
examples.trans: Listen, Samson, I've been thinking. Your boss is such an experienced specialist.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to know'.

examples.trans: I don't know.
As you all know...

examples.text: Спасибо, спасибо! Как вы все знаете, я родился и вырос в Синеозерске.
examples.trans: Thank you, thank you! As you all know, I was born and grew up in Sineozersk.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'where', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Where's my toy car?
Where's Dad?

examples.text: А где машинка? Где моя машинка?
examples.trans: Hey, where's the toy car? Where's my toy car?

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'shorts' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Слушай, Саша, ты не знаешь, где мои шорты?
examples.trans: Listen, Sasha, do you know where my shorts are?

examples.text: На нашей кухне уже есть новый шорты.
examples.trans: In our kitchen there is already a new shorts.

meanings.note: Prefix 'пред-' ('before, fore-') indicates anticipation or prior position (stem 'ставлять'). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to imagine; to introduce, present', paired with 'представить'.

examples.trans: Can you believe it, they forgot it in the oven!

examples.text: Ты даже не представляешь, как я устал.
examples.trans: You can't even imagine how tired I am.

examples.text: Представляешь, в духовке забыли! Юль, выйди.
examples.trans: Can you believe it, they forgot it in the oven! Yul, step out.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'everything, all; that's it', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Everything's fine.
That's it, bye!

examples.text: Мы просто не хотели вас беспокоить. Всё отменим!
examples.trans: We just didn't want to bother you. We'll cancel it all!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronominal determiner meaning 'your', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Я бы на твоём месте подумал.
examples.trans: If I were you, I'd think about it.

examples.text: Слушай, Самсон, я тут подумал. Твой начальник — такой опытный специалист.
examples.trans: Listen, Samson, I've been thinking. Your boss is such an experienced specialist.
Your boss is such an experienced specialist.

meanings.note: Common feminine noun meaning 'thing' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: I've brought you your things.
Where are my things?
Everyone has one of these.

meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'меститься'). Reflexive/intransitive verb with the postfix '-ся'/'-сь' (historically from the reflexive pronoun 'себя', oneself). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to fit in'.

related.gloss: not to to fit in (negated infinitive)

examples.text: Представляешь, все твои вещи поместились здесь.
examples.trans: Can you imagine, all of your things fit right in here.

examples.text: На кухне никто не хочет поместиться без причины.
examples.trans: In the kitchen nobody wants to fit in without a reason.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'here', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: I'm here.
We live here.
But we're in business here.
